A Python Enhancement Proposal lists this idea as rejected:
Title: Mark a base class to force explicit overrides on subclasses
Text: We considered including a class decorator @require_explicit_overrides, which would have provided a way for base classes to declare that all subclasses must use the @override decorator on method overrides. The Overrides library has a mixin class, EnforceExplicitOverrides, which provides similar behavior in runtime checks. We decided against this because we expect owners of large codebases will benefit most from @override, and for these use cases having a strict mode where explicit @override is required (see the Backward Compatibility section) provides more benefits than a way to mark base classes. Moreover we believe that authors of projects who do not consider the extra type safety to be worth the additional boilerplate of using @override should not be forced to do so. Having an optional strict mode puts the decision in the hands of project owners, whereas the use of @require_explicit_overrides in libraries would force project owners to use @override even if they prefer not to.

Ideas found by reading the public discussion:
0. Requiring the decorator specifically for abstract method overrides (rejected in favor of a strict mode option) [rejected] - The idea of adding a specific mode or flag to require the decorator only for abstract methods was turned down. Reasons: I'm not sure there is much need for special treatment of abstract methods. The PEP recommends type checkers support a strict mode where all method overrides must be marked with the decorator, whether abstract or not.
1. Rejecting built-in runtime enforcement or parent-class specification due to low utility and library-level implementability [rejected] - The proposal to allow specifying the exact base class was rejected due to low utility and implementation complexity. Reasons: if in a single commit you move a method from one base to another, you as the author are likely aware of what you did, so the safety benefits are relatively small; I'm guessing there wouldn't be too much use of this feature. Since it's relatively easy to implement this capability using runtime logic in a library, that makes me thing we don't need to bake it into typing.py all of the type checkers.
2. Accepted proposals: providing a TYPE_CHECKING shim for third-party decorators and adopting the main @typing.override decorator [accepted] - A pattern was proposed and accepted to allow third-party libraries to define their own override decorators that mimic the standard one. Reasons: One way of handling this kind of thing is to do a typing.TYPE_CHECKING shim, like so: from typing import TYPE_CHECKING if TYPE_CHECKING: from typing import override as override else: def override(func):; The SC has decided to accept this PEP!

best: the number of the idea that is the SAME idea as the rejected one, or -1 if none of them is.
reasons_agree: if there is a match, do its reasons agree with the reason the proposal gives?
"yes" (same reason), "partial" (overlapping), "no" (different). If best is -1, answer "no".
